posts.title: Philadelphia Spent 25 Years Saying Yes to Cameras. Here's My No Vote.
posts.dek: How red-light and speed cameras quietly became citywide, and why I think the program deserves the debate it never got.
posts.author: Philly Rivers
posts.summary: Philadelphia built a quarter-century of automated red-light and speed enforcement on near-unanimous votes and almost no public debate. A personal case for slowing down.
posts.content_md:
My wife has never run a red light in her life. The city has two photographs that say otherwise.

Both were taken at the same intersection, Walnut Lane and Henry Avenue, while she was turning left onto Ridge. It's a turn we've made a hundred times, the same turn millions of Americans make every day. Both times there was no oncoming traffic. Both times the light ran its entire cycle while the car was already committed to the turn: green, a blink of yellow, red. Quicker than any honest yellow should be, and faster than felt fair. No screech of brakes. No near-miss. Nobody in the crosswalk, nobody anywhere close to harm. Just a flash from a box on a pole and, a few weeks later, two $100 demands in the mail.

Two hundred dollars poorer for a maneuver that hurt no one.

Here's the part I can't shake: I still get a knot of anxiety every single time I drive through that light. Not because the intersection is dangerous, since it isn't, but because I know the machine is up there, waiting, and I know there is nothing I can say to it. No officer who watched it happen and weighed whether we'd actually done anything wrong. No hearing where I get to point out that the yellow was too short to clear the turn legally. No one to argue with, no discretion to appeal to, no human who decided we were a danger that day. Just a threshold, a photograph, and a bill.

Then, a few months later, they got her again. A speed camera this time, on Broad Street. Her offense: driving one of the widest, straightest, most forgiving stretches of road in the city at the speed the road all but invites. The limit on Broad is 25, a number set so far below how the street actually drives that just about everyone on it is a ticket waiting to be printed. We didn't even know Broad was being clocked; there was no real sign, nothing that registered as a warning that a machine was measuring our speed. Just, a few weeks later, the same envelope: another $100, another photograph, another moment that put no one in danger.

Set a limit that far under the natural speed of a road and you're not calibrating for safety. Thirty-five would do that honestly. You're stocking the pond.

We paid them, all three, three hundred dollars for three moments that hurt nobody. I was angry. And then I did the thing I always tell other people to do: I went and read the actual legislative record. I run a site that tracks every bill Philadelphia City Council has passed since 2000, so I have the receipts. I expected to find a contentious fight: surveillance versus safety, the kind of debate a city is supposed to have before it points cameras at its own residents.

I found almost nothing. And *that* is what turned my anger into opposition.

## The receipts: 25 years of yes

Philadelphia runs two automated-enforcement programs, and the legislative trail is remarkably one-sided.

The **red-light camera** program came first. In November 2000, Council passed [the enabling ordinance](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_1225120) creating civil liability for camera-caught red-light running, a $100 fine issued from a photograph. Over the next two decades, Council came back to amend, extend, and expand that program **dozens of times**, intersection by intersection. I went through the votes. They are almost uniformly 16–0 and 17–0. As recently as December 2025, Council was still [adding new red-light cameras](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_251068), this time at School House Lane and Henry Avenue.

The **speed-camera** program is newer and moving faster. In 2019, Council [created a new chapter of the city code](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_3889635), "Use of an Automated Speed Enforcement System," to put cameras on Roosevelt Boulevard, with tiered fines of $100, $125, and $150 for drivers caught going 11 mph or more over the limit. For a few years that was the whole program: one notoriously deadly road.

Then, in the span of about eighteen months, it became everything:

- May 2024: [Speed cameras on Broad Street](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_6663192)
- October 2024: [Speed cameras expanded across Philly streets](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_7005048)
- February 2025: [Speed cameras in school zones](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_7158344)
- September 2025: [Speed cameras on state routes](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_7664638)

Every one of those passed unanimously, or close to it.

## Nobody said no

Here is the single fact that bothers me most. In twenty-five years of Council building out an automated surveillance-and-fine apparatus that now spans red lights, boulevards, school zones, and state routes, I can find essentially **one dissenting vote**.

On that original 2000 red-light bill, the vote was 15–1. The lone "no" belonged to Councilmember Cohen. After that, the record goes quiet. Bill after bill, year after year, the cameras expanded and the tally was unanimous.

I want to be fair about what that does and doesn't mean. Unanimity can signal genuine consensus on something that obviously works. But it can also signal that a program stopped being *debated*, that "more cameras" became a default, a routine line-item nobody campaigns against because the alternative is to look soft on a child getting hit on the Boulevard.

When a city expands surveillance of its own residents for a quarter century without a single sustained argument against it on the record, that's not a settled debate. That's an *absent* one. So consider this my no vote, cast late.

## The honest case for the cameras

I'm not going to strawman the other side, because the other side has real points and I'd be lying if I pretended otherwise.

Roosevelt Boulevard earned its cameras. It has been one of the most dangerous roads in Pennsylvania for decades, a twelve-lane river of traffic running through dense neighborhoods, with a death toll to match. After automated enforcement went in, speeds and crashes on the corridor fell sharply. If you believe a policy should be judged by whether it stops people from dying, the Boulevard is the strongest argument the cameras have, and it is a strong one.

The deeper point is this: a camera doesn't get tired, doesn't profile, and doesn't escalate a stop into a tragedy. We have spent years, rightly, worrying about what happens when an armed officer pulls over a driver for going 9 over. A camera never pulls anyone over. It never asks you to step out of the vehicle. For a city trying to reduce dangerous police-citizen encounters, "let the machine handle speeding" is not a crazy answer. It might even be a humane one.

I take all of that seriously. It's why this is hard.

## Why I still oppose it

And yet.

**The money never sleeps.** A fine is a tax that we only call a fine because a machine caught you. Once a city wires part of its budget to violations, it acquires an interest in violations *continuing*: in thresholds staying low, in yellow lights staying short, in "just one more corridor." I'm not alleging a conspiracy. I'm pointing at an incentive, and incentives win in the long run. A safety program that would celebrate its own obsolescence is trustworthy. A revenue program that needs you to keep speeding is not.

**Mission creep is the whole story.** Look back at that timeline. We started with one deadly boulevard and a narrow justification almost no one could argue with. We ended, within a few years, with cameras as the city's general-purpose enforcement tool. The [May 2024 vote that put a speed camera on Broad Street](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_6663192), the same one that eventually mailed my wife a $100 ticket for driving Broad the way Broad is built to be driven, passed **17–0**. Not one member rose to ask whether a 25 mph limit on that road was protecting anyone or simply printing money. There was even a [2020 proposal to add automated license-plate readers](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_4681897) to the mix, which is a different thing entirely: not catching a dangerous act, but logging where your car is. Each step was small. Each step used the credibility of the last. That's how surveillance infrastructure always gets built. Not in one vote you can rally against, but in twenty you never hear about.

**And the cameras still don't fix the road.** Slower cars are safer cars, and the Boulevard's numbers are real. I won't pretend otherwise. But a camera polices speed, not design, and a twelve-lane highway run through row-home neighborhoods stays lethal no matter how many photographs it takes. On August 28, 2025, five years into the program, [a single crash](https://www.inquirer.com/news/philadelphia/roosevelt-boulevard-vehicle-crash-pedestrians-killed-20250828.html) on the 9000 block of East Roosevelt Boulevard killed a driver and a pedestrian and left a third person in critical condition. Meanwhile the deadliest road in the city in 2024 [wasn't the Boulevard at all, it was Broad Street](https://www.phillyvoice.com/vision-zero-report-2024-traffic-deaths-broad-street/), at more than a fatality a month: the same Broad Street where the city's answer was to mail my wife a ticket for doing a few miles an hour over an invented limit. When enforcement clusters where the fines come easy instead of where the dying is worst, you have to ask what problem it was really built to solve.

**Automated justice removes the human.** The thing I hated about those tickets was never really the money. It was that there was no one in the loop. Due process used to mean a person had to look at you and decide. Now the decision is a threshold and the appeal is a web form. We should be slow, genuinely slow, to remove human judgment from the act of the government penalizing a citizen, even when the human was imperfect. *Especially* then.

**And the debate never happened.** Even if every camera in this city is justified, we deserved the argument. We deserved a Council that made the case out loud, weighed the privacy cost in public, and put a real check on expansion. Instead we got unanimity and silence, and a program that grew while no one was watching it watch us.

## What I'd actually want

I'm not anti-safety, and I'm not naive enough to think the Boulevard should go back to being a speedway. So here's what accountable automated enforcement would look like to me:

1. **Revenue-neutral by design.** Fines fund traffic safety and nothing else; any surplus triggers a rate cut, not a new corridor. Break the budget's dependence on violations.
2. **Sunset clauses.** Every camera authorization expires and must be re-justified with crash data, not renewed by default. Make Council vote *yes* again on purpose.
3. **A hard wall against the LPR creep.** Speed and red-light enforcement is one debate. Mass location tracking is another, and it should never ride in on the first one's coattails.
4. **A real appeal, heard by a person.** If the city is going to penalize you by photograph, you get a human being to contest it in front of, easily and for free.

None of that is anti-camera. It's pro-debate. It's the conversation Philadelphia skipped twenty-five years ago and has been skipping ever since.

We paid our tickets. I'd just like to think the city had to *earn* them, and that next time, somebody on Council says what I'm saying here, before the vote instead of a resident saying it after.

posts.title: They Raised My Assessment to Pay for Schools. Then They Closed 17 of Them.
posts.dek: Philadelphia reassessed my home, sent most of the bill to the School District, and octupled its own school funding. Here's what that money is buying, and what it isn't.
posts.author: Philly Rivers
posts.summary: Most of your Philadelphia property tax is a school tax, and the city has octupled its own school funding since 2018. Yet the district spends $22,000 a student, posts 25% math proficiency, and just voted to close 17 schools. A parent-taxpayer follows the money.
posts.content_md:
I'd like to be able to send my kids to the public school down the street. Not some lifelong dream. Just a reasonable expectation for a family that pays what we pay to live here. With a second one due in a couple of weeks, where they'll go to school has stopped being a someday question.

So let me tell you what's happened to my tax bill while I've been weighing it.

For years, the city figured my rowhome in East Falls was worth about $250,000. Then, in the span of three tax years, the Office of Property Assessment decided it was worth **$461,000**, a jump of more than **80%**. What actually hits your wallet is the *taxable* value, market value minus the Homestead Exemption, and mine went from **$173,000 in 2024 to $361,000 in 2027. It more than doubled.** At the city's 1.3998% rate, my bill climbed from roughly **$2,400 a year to about $5,050**, for the exact same house, on the exact same block, that I already owned.

Notice the quiet part, too: the Homestead Exemption that's supposed to protect me is a flat dollar amount. It crept from $80,000 to $100,000 while my assessed value exploded by more than $200,000. A fixed shield against a soaring number isn't much of a shield.

I'm not a special case. Philadelphia has reassessed again and again, a citywide jump averaging **31%** in 2023 and another round in 2025, and for plenty of us the taxable value has simply run away from the paycheck. Every year or two the number goes up, and there's nothing you can do about the value they assign your home except pay it.

So I did the thing I always do: I followed the money. Where does a Philadelphia property-tax dollar actually go? The answer surprised me, and then it worried me, because most of it goes to schools, and I'm no longer sure the schools are worth what we're being charged.

## Your property tax is mostly a school tax

Philadelphia's real estate tax rate is **1.3998%**. But that number is split: **0.6159% goes to the City and 0.7839% goes to the School District.** As of this year the schools' share is **56%**; the city keeps 44%.

So when they reassess your home and your bill jumps, the *majority* of that increase isn't paving your street or keeping your library open. It's going to the School District of Philadelphia.

And that's just the property-tax piece. Separately, the city has been shoveling its own general-fund money into schools. I pulled 25 years of city budgets into a [budget explorer](/budget), and the line called "Contribution to School District" went from **$35 million in 2008, to $178 million in 2019, to $284 million today**, an eightfold increase. Most of that ramp came after 2018, when the schools returned to local control and the city took ownership of the results.

Add it up and the message is unmistakable: your rising tax bill is, first and foremost, a bet on Philadelphia's schools.

Which leaves exactly one question that matters. **Are we winning that bet?**

## $22,000 a child, and one in four can do grade-level math

Here's where it gets hard.

Philadelphia now spends about **$22,379 per student** per year. That is not a low number. It's higher than plenty of the suburban districts people move to *for the schools.*

And here's what that money buys, by the district's own reporting:

- **25% of students in grades 3–8 are proficient in math.** Three out of four are not.
- **33% are proficient in reading**, and that number went *down* last year.
- The four-year graduation rate is **77.5%**, better than it was, but still nearly one in four kids not finishing on time.

The district's own goal is to reach 52% math proficiency by 2030. They're at 25. That's not an ambitious target; it's an admission of how deep the hole is.

I want to be fair here, because this is genuinely complicated:

- Philadelphia educates a very high-poverty student body, and poverty is the single strongest predictor of test scores anywhere in America. Comparing Philly's raw numbers to a wealthy suburb isn't apples to apples.
- The district was starved for years: a state takeover from 2001 to 2018, chronic underfunding, and in 2023 a Pennsylvania court ruled the *state's* school-funding system unconstitutional. Philly is genuinely shortchanged by Harrisburg.
- The numbers are, slowly, moving the right way. Math is up from its pandemic low. Graduation is up.

All true. And I *still* can't get past the core of it: I'm being asked to pay more every year, into a system that graduates a quarter of its kids late and can't get most of them to grade level, and to simply trust that this time the money will land.

## Then they closed 17 schools

While I was staring at my new assessment, the School Board voted, **6 to 3, on April 30**, to close **17 schools.**

Not because the checkbook hit zero on paper. It's part of a **$3 billion facilities plan** to shutter aging, under-enrolled buildings and modernize others. But the timing tells you plenty: it lands right as **$1.2 billion in federal COVID relief money runs out**, the same temporary federal wave you can watch crest and recede in the city's own budget numbers. Most of City Council threatened to block the closures. The board did it anyway.

So here's the view from my kitchen table: my assessment goes up, most of it flows to the schools, the city has octupled its own school funding, we spend $22,000 a child, and what my kids are offered in return is a closed building and a one-in-four shot at grade-level math.

## Notice what the city funded, and what it didn't

One more thing I found in the budget that I can't unsee.

The **Office of Property Assessment**, the office whose entire job is to raise your home's value, has roughly **doubled** its budget over the last decade, to about **$22 million**. Meanwhile the **Board of Revision of Taxes**, the office where you go to *appeal* your assessment, has sat flat at about **$1.1 million for fifteen years.**

The city invested in the machine that raises your number. It did not invest in the process that lets you fight it. That's a choice, and it tells you exactly who the system is built to serve.

## What you can actually do about your bill

I'm angry, but I'm also practical, and if your assessment jumped, there are real ways to lower what you owe. Do these:

- **Homestead Exemption.** If you own and live in your home, this knocks **$100,000** off your assessed value before the tax is calculated. The city just raised it from $80,000. If you haven't applied, do it today; for most homeowners it's the single biggest lever.
- **First Level Review and formal appeal.** You can ask the city to review your new assessment, and separately appeal to the Board of Revision of Taxes. Deadlines are strict, so check the date on your notice.
- **LOOP (Longtime Owner Occupants Program).** If you've owned your home 10+ years and your assessment spiked, this can cap the increase, but you generally can't combine it with the Homestead Exemption, so compare which saves you more.
- **Senior Citizen Tax Freeze.** If you're 65+ and income-eligible, this locks your bill so future reassessments can't push it up.
- **Payment plans.** If the bill is a true hardship, the city offers installment and hardship options. Don't just fall behind. Call.

Details and applications are on the city's [Real Estate Tax page](https://www.phila.gov/services/payments-assistance-taxes/taxes/property-and-real-estate-taxes/real-estate-tax/).

## The bottom line

I'm not against funding schools. I'd just like the school down the street to be good enough that sending my kids there is an easy call. That's the whole reason I'm holding this bill up to the light instead of paying it and moving on.

Because the deal on the table right now is: pay more, every year, forever, into a system that's closing schools and can't get three out of four kids to grade level, and don't ask too many questions. That's not a deal. That's a demand.

I'll keep paying. But I want what anyone wants when the price keeps climbing: proof it's working. Show me the reading scores rising. Show me the schools staying open. Show me my kids have a seat worth having. Until then, every reassessment notice is going to feel less like an investment in my city and more like a bill for a service I'm not receiving.

---

*Sources: Philadelphia [2023 reassessment (avg +31%)](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/philadelphia/philadelphia-property-tax-assessments-increase-mayor-jim-kenney-20220503.html) and [2025 reassessment (+$330, 56% school share)](https://www.phillyvoice.com/philly-property-tax-increase-reassessment-2025/); [test scores](https://billypenn.com/2025/10/22/philadelphia-public-schools-math-reading-test-scores-preliminary-data/); [graduation rate](https://www.philasd.org/blog/2024/11/21/student-enrollment-and-4-year-graduation-rate-increases/); [per-pupil spending](https://www.inquirer.com/news/philadelphia-school-district-2024-budget-dropouts-20230421.html); [the 17-school closure vote](https://whyy.org/articles/philadelphia-school-board-closure-vote/). City budget figures are from Open Common Ground's own [budget explorer](/budget), parsed from Philadelphia's annual appropriation ordinances.*

posts.title: An E-Bike Nearly Ran Me Down. I Went Looking for the Rules and Found Five Dead Bills.
posts.dek: Philadelphia already has rules for cyclists. What it has never done is vote on them: five bills since 2000 died in committee without a roll call, and so did 1,624 others. Here is what I would enforce instead, and why I think it would pass.
posts.author: Philly Rivers
posts.summary: Five Council bills between 2006 and 2015 would have imposed registration, fines, forfeiture or a mandatory lane duty on cyclists. All five lapsed without a recorded vote, while every bill regulating drivers in bike lanes passed unanimously. Pennsylvania's crash database only counts collisions involving a motor vehicle, so a cyclist striking a pedestrian is recorded nowhere. The 2026 e-bike delivery licence bill explicitly creates no plate and changes no traffic rule.
posts.content_md:
I was picking my wife up from a hair appointment at 17th and Sansom when I watched a delivery rider on an e-bike thread between two moving cars, blow the red at the corner, and keep going. He was not the only one. A few weeks later, walking to meet a friend, one of them nearly took me out on the sidewalk. He did not flinch or turn around. No "sorry," no "excuse me." I stood there with my heart pounding.

So I did what I always do when something in this city makes me angry. I went and read the law.

I run a site that tracks every bill introduced in Philadelphia City Council since 2000. I assumed I would find the city had never bothered to write the rules. What I found was stranger, and it changed what I think the problem is.

## Five bills, zero votes

Here is every bill since 2000 that would have added a new duty, penalty, registration requirement or forfeiture for people riding bicycles.

- **2006, bill 060897** (DiCicco). Would have barred pedalcycles seating more than two passengers from roadways.
- **2009, bill 090845** (DiCicco). Would have required registration of every bicycle ridden on a public right of way.
- **2009, bills 090829 and 090828** (Kenney). Would have raised the fines in the city's bicycle chapter. The second would also have let the city seize bikes without working brakes.
- **2015, bill 150617** (Oh). Would have required cyclists to ride in a bike lane wherever one exists.

For all five, the vote record is empty at every stage. They were introduced, sent to committee, and left there until the term ran out.

That is not unusual, and the real number is worse. Of the 8,465 bills introduced from 2000 through 2025, 1,624, about one in five, lapsed without a single recorded vote. Nobody conspired to bury the cyclist rules. They went into the same drawer as sixteen hundred other bills, which is its own indictment.

So no member of Council has ever had to go on the record about new penalties for cyclists. If that makes you angry, there is nobody to vote out over it, because nobody ever voted.

## What I want, up front

Three behaviors enforced: riding the wrong way up a one-way, riding on the sidewalk, and running red lights. A number on commercial delivery bikes that can be read off the bike, so a rider who does those things repeatedly can lose the right to do them for money. Nothing for the commuter, the kid or the weekend rider. And all of it paired with something that costs drivers, because that is the only kind of cyclist rule this city has ever passed.

I am not asking for a crackdown on cyclists. By the end I will have argued against several things I believed when I started, including that one.

## What Council will vote on

Five bike bills did pass, all unanimously: [sidewalk riding designations](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_1233630) in 2009, 16 to 0; [Complete Streets](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_1236508) in 2012, 17 to 0; [removing abandoned bicycles](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_2259800) in 2015, 15 to 0; [licensing bike share](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_3493790) in 2018, 17 to 0; and [no stopping or parking in a bike lane](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_6851748) in 2024, 17 to 0.

Look at who each one binds: drivers, bike share companies, abandoned frames, and one that permits sidewalk riding rather than restricting it. Only Complete Streets sets rules for how cyclists ride, and it came bundled with new obligations on drivers. Not one imposes a standalone new penalty on a rider.

The clearest case is Oh's 2015 bill. It would have required cyclists to use bike lanes and raised penalties on drivers who block them. It lapsed. Nine years later Council passed the driver half on its own, 17 to 0. The cyclist half never came back. Records show outcomes, not motives, so I cannot tell you anyone split that bill on purpose. But the half aimed at drivers is law, and the half aimed at riders is not.

## The rules exist. The consequences don't.

That is the part I had wrong. Pennsylvania law gives a person on a bicycle "all of the duties applicable to the driver of a vehicle." Red lights and stop signs bind a rider exactly as they bind me in my car, and riders must go with traffic. Philadelphia goes further: its code allows sidewalk riding only for children under 12, and not even for them in a business district. The man who nearly ran me down was not in a gray area.

A legal e-bike, meaning under 100 pounds, with working pedals, a motor of 750 watts or less and a top assisted speed of 20 miles per hour, counts as a bicycle: no plate, no registration, no insurance. Anything beyond that is an unregistered motor vehicle, and the registration rules people assume do not exist have applied all along.

Pennsylvania even used to require cyclists to use a bike lane where one was available. The legislature dropped that in 1998. Oh's bill would have restored it for Philadelphia.

What is missing is a consequence. Breaking the city's bicycle rules carries a fine of up to $75, and collecting it takes an officer who sees the violation, stops the rider and writes the ticket. A driver 11 miles an hour over on Roosevelt Boulevard gets a $100 ticket generated by a camera and mailed home. Philadelphia [automated enforcement against drivers](/blog/philadelphia-automated-enforcement) and left the cyclist rules to a traffic stop that essentially never happens. It runs the other way too: state law requires drivers to give cyclists four feet when passing, and you can ask anyone who rides how often that is enforced.

## The number nobody collects

If delivery riders are as dangerous as they feel, that should show up somewhere. It doesn't, because of one line of state law. Pennsylvania's crash database counts a crash only if at least one motor vehicle in transport was involved, and a bicycle does not count as one.

So an e-bike hit by a car is in the data. An e-bike that hits a pedestrian is not. In Philadelphia in 2025, according to PennDOT data reported by the Inquirer, e-bikes and e-scooters were involved in 197 crashes, with four riders killed and 193 injured, up about 40 percent from 2024. Every one of those crashes involved a motor vehicle; that is what got them counted. Had the rider on the sidewalk actually hit me, the collision would not have entered the state's crash database at all.

A police report might exist, or a hospital record. What does not exist is the thing a legislator would need: a steady count of pedestrians hurt by people on bikes. You cannot legislate against a number nobody collects.

## The other half, which I am not going to skip

On July 13, 2024, I was riding home from a haircut on Main Street in Manayunk when a car parked at the curb pulled out in front of me. I hit the side of it, went over the bars and landed hard on my right side. I got up, told the driver and a rider who stopped that I was fine, and forgave the driver. Nobody called police. I did not go to a hospital. A car pulling out of a parking space is a motor vehicle in transport, and I was hurt, so that crash should have been reportable. It is in no dataset anywhere. I am one of the holes in the number I was asking for, and what survives into the data is the severe end of it.

Four days later, on July 17, Dr. Barbara Friedes, a 30-year-old pediatric resident at Children's Hospital, was riding in the Spruce Street bike lane at 18th when a drunk driver struck and killed her. That is a few blocks from where I watched the delivery riders. She was wearing a helmet. She was where she was supposed to be. The lane was paint and flexible plastic posts.

The city's answer was to make that lane physical: concrete separators, plus loading zones carved out of residential permit parking so delivery vehicles would have somewhere to stop besides the bike lane. Neighbors sued. Friends of Pine and Spruce incorporated in January 2025 and filed suit that June, arguing the city could not reassign parking without an ordinance from Council. That September the Society Hill Civic Association board voted to give the group $25,000 toward legal costs. A judge paused the work, and in July 2026 the court refused to let it resume. The concrete has not been poured.

I never rode on the sidewalk, and I am not writing this as someone who thinks cyclists are the problem. Thirty-nine people died in Philadelphia traffic in the first half of 2025 alone, in crashes involving motor vehicles. A cyclist running a red light is a hazard. A driver running one is operating two tons of machinery. Cyclists behaving badly is not an argument for leaving cyclists unprotected, and the clearest illustration of that is three blocks from where I was standing.

## It is not the fix

When I first read about [bill 260525](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_8029005), I assumed it was the fix. It would have Licenses and Inspections issue an E-Bike Delivery License to anyone delivering by e-bike, and its companion, [260526](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_8029006), would make delivery companies keep a registry of their riders. Both are Councilmember Young's, and both are still in committee.

Then I read the text. The license "shall not constitute a vehicle title, vehicle registration, driver's license, license plate, inspection certificate, insurance requirement, or other authorization to operate a pedalcycle with electric assist." No plate, nothing on the bike to read. The registry "shall not require a covered delivery worker to obtain a City license" and changes no traffic rule.

There is one real lever. The city could revoke a license for "repeated violations of this Chapter while performing commercial delivery service," and that chapter is the bicycle rules. But somebody has to write those citations first, and essentially nobody does. And the bill reaches only commercial riders, people paid per delivery, many of them immigrants, represented by nobody. After a quarter century of declining to regulate cyclists, the first serious attempt lands on the riders with the least power to object.

## The version I would vote for

I am not against 260525. I am against mistaking it for a solution.

Put a numbered tag on the machine, issued by the city to commercial delivery riders the way a vendor cart or a taxi carries one. Not a PennDOT plate, and nothing for the commuter, the kid or the weekend rider. Tie revocation to the three behaviors that matter: wrong-way riding, sidewalk riding and running reds. Fund someone to enforce it. And pair it, in the same bill, with something that costs drivers, the way the 2012 Complete Streets bill did. I cannot prove bundling is why that one passed while the others died, but it is the only cyclist conduct rule in twenty-six years that made it through.

The details will not be simple: how an officer identifies a repeat offender, how a rider appeals a ticket he did not earn, how to keep it from becoming a pretext for stopping people. A city can work through those, and none of them is a reason to keep doing nothing.

Do that and I think it passes 17 to 0, like everything else here. And if a rule is right, it should be right for the lawyer on a Specialized too.

Leave the bill as written and Council gets to say it addressed e-bikes, the riders get a card in their wallet, the guy who nearly ran me down keeps riding exactly as he did, and in five years somebody writes this same column again.

## What to watch

- **[Bills 260525](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_8029005) and [260526](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_8029006)** are still in committee. This is when the scope can change.
- **[Bill 250649](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_7436536)**, the bike lane around City Hall, passed Council 17 to 0 on October 15 and is on the mayor's desk.
- **[Bill 260699](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_8216670)**, filed in September, would reduce automated speed-camera fines based on how far over the limit a driver was. Keep the cameras, soften the penalty on drivers.

The record is public and searchable. You do not have to take my reading of it. [Go look](/philadelphia/insights/what-dies).

Philadelphia e-bike and e-scooter crash counts for 2025 from PennDOT, [as reported by the Inquirer](https://www.inquirer.com/transportation/ebike-escooters-deadly-crashes-philadelphia-20260714.html) in July 2026. Fatality counts for the first half of 2025 from the [Bicycle Coalition of Greater Philadelphia](https://bicyclecoalition.org/traffic-fatalities-see-a-decrease-in-the-first-6-months-of-2025/). The Pine and Spruce lawsuit from [WHYY](https://whyy.org/articles/philadelphia-bike-lanes-lawsuit/), the Inquirer's reporting on [the Society Hill vote](https://www.inquirer.com/transportation/society-hill-vote-block-bike-lanes-20250918.html), and [the July 2026 ruling](https://www.inquirer.com/transportation/neighbors-suit-judge-continues-pause-on-pine-spruce-bike-lane-upgrades-20260713.html). posts.title: A Councilmember Plans to Retire Between Terms and Collect $350,000. Three Bills Would Have Stopped It. None Got a Vote.
posts.dek: Philadelphia closed DROP to elected officials in 2010 but let everyone already in office keep it. Three earlier bills would have closed it to them too. None got a vote, and neither did 23 more on the rules for the city's own elected officials.
posts.author: Philly Rivers
posts.summary: Three bills that would have kept sitting Philadelphia officials out of DROP died without a vote, and so did 23 more on hiring relatives, outside income, term limits, public financing and a redistricting commission. Rules for donors, contractors, lobbyists and gift-givers all eventually passed on recorded votes.
posts.content_md:
In June I read in the Inquirer that Councilmember Curtis Jones plans to retire in December 2027, right after the November election, and, if he is reelected, be sworn into a new term in January 2028. Retiring between terms lets him collect a lump sum from the city's Deferred Retirement Option Plan, which he told the paper would come to closer to $350,000.

DROP lets a city worker who is eligible to retire commit to leaving within four years, while the pension payments they would have received pile up in an account they collect on the way out. For most workers, leaving means leaving. For an official who just won reelection, it can mean a short break between terms.

I did not know that was legal. Did you? In 2010 Jones voted for the law that closed DROP to future elected officials. Everyone already serving, including him, kept it. He is doing what that law allows. He is not the point of this. The law is.

So I looked up how that law was written, and kept going.

## Three bills would have stopped it

Four times, members of Council proposed keeping elected officials out of DROP. None of the four got a vote.

- **2004, Michael Nutter ([040269](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_1227995)).** Barred officials who first took office on or after January 2, 2006. Jones took office in 2008.
- **2008, Bill Green ([080020](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_1232233)).** Barred elected officials, except those already enrolled or with eight years of city service. Jones was a co-sponsor.
- **2009, Jim Kenney ([090209](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_1233395)).** One sentence: "No elected official shall be eligible to participate in the DROP program."
- **2010, Marian Tasco ([100542](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_1234685)).** Would have ended DROP for everyone not already in it.

Nutter's, Kenney's and Tasco's would each have kept Jones out.

The bill that did pass, [100095](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_1234237), went through 17 to 0 in 2010 because the state required it. Its title says it was "conforming the City's DROP program to the requirements of Pennsylvania Act No. 44 of 2009." And Council's version let everyone already in office keep DROP.

A year later Council voted to keep the program itself. In June 2011 one committee heard Tasco's bill to end DROP and [a bill to keep it](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_1235480) with lower costs. The second passed. When Mayor Nutter vetoed it because he wanted DROP gone, Council overrode him 17 to 0. Tasco's bill never came back.

## It is not just DROP

I sorted every bill introduced from 2000 through 2023 that changed a rule for the city's elected officials by subject, and checked which subjects ever got a recorded vote. Five never did, on any bill: hiring relatives, outside jobs and income, term limits, public money for campaigns, and a redistricting commission.

That is 23 bills. With the four DROP bills, it is 27, from 11 members over two decades. About one Philadelphia bill in five dies without a recorded vote. On these six subjects it was 27 of 28, and the 28th was the one the state required.

If you want to know where your councilmember stands on hiring relatives, there is no vote to look up.

## What I want, up front

Two things. First, a recorded vote on the anti-nepotism bill, pass or fail, with seventeen names attached. Councilmembers hire their own staff outside civil service, and as far as I can find, no city law specifically stops them from hiring relatives. Second, a change to Council's rules so every bill on these subjects gets a recorded vote of the full Council before the term ends.

I am not saying Council is corrupt, or that anyone is hiding from these bills on purpose. The record shows what happened, not why.

## The 23 bills

- **Hiring relatives: seven bills, 2001 to 2008,** four from Nutter, two from Frank Rizzo Jr. and one from Jannie Blackwell. Nutter's [2001 version](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_1225999) treated "the Mayor, the City Controller, and members of Council" as controlling every city office, so none of them could recommend a relative for a city job. It cleared committee in April 2003 and was placed on the calendar for a final vote, but it was never called up. The term ended and it died.
- **Outside jobs and income: three bills.** Rizzo Jr. in 2007 and 2008, and Maria Quiñones Sánchez in [2021](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_5363253), whose bill would have capped a councilmember's outside earned income at $25,000 a year.
- **Term limits: five bills.** W. Wilson Goode Jr. proposed three terms for Council in 2010. Allan Domb proposed four in [2020](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_4314034) and 2022, counting only terms that began in 2024, so no sitting member would have been barred before 2040. Even that version never got a vote. Council President Darrell Clarke's two 2020 bills covered Council, the Controller, the City Commissioners and the Sheriff.
- **Public money for campaigns: seven bills.** Kenney in 2007, then Derek Green five times between 2017 and 2022, two of them ballot questions that would only have asked voters whether Council should adopt it.
- **A redistricting commission: one bill,** from Derek Green in [2022](/philadelphia/legislation/legistar_phila_5570930).

## What did get votes

On five other ethics subjects, Council passed laws, and every one got recorded votes along the way. Contribution limits passed in 2003 over Mayor John Street's veto, after an earlier version lost on the floor 7 to 10. Pay-to-play limits on city contracts passed in 2005, after an earlier version tied 7 to 7. An independent Board of Ethics went to voters 16 to 0 in 2005, along with its powers, including mandatory ethics training. Lobbyist registration passed 17 to 0 in 2010. A gift ban passed 15 to 0 in 2014. Five subjects, five laws, and even the losses were on the record.

Most bills that made the job easier got votes too. In 2003 Council raised elected officials' pay and tied future raises to inflation, overriding Street 12 to 4. The yearly raises since have come without a vote. Council voted in 2006 and again in 2014 to ask voters to drop the resign-to-run rule, which makes city officials give up their seats to run for other offices, overriding Nutter's veto the second time. Voters said no both times. A couple died without one.

## My reading

Several of the laws that passed bind members. Contribution limits cap what they raise, the gift ban limits what they accept, and the Board of Ethics polices them. Council has also voted to extend its family ethics rules to life partners, to strengthen its ban on retaliation, and to ask voters to make district members live in their districts. Council does pass rules on itself.

But the rules that passed regulate what comes toward the office: money, gifts, lobbyists, contracts. The bills that never got a vote would have changed the office itself: who works in it, what else its holder earns, how long anyone holds it, who draws its lines, how campaigns for it are paid for, and what it pays out at the end. When Council did change pensions for elected officials, in 2010 and 2014, the changes applied to people elected later.

That is my reading, not a finding. I picked the six subjects after seeing which ones never got a vote, and you can draw the line differently. The full list is linked below so you can.

## Arguing with myself

Dying without a vote is normal here. One bill in five does: 1,624 of the 7,890 introduced from 2000 through 2023. Some of these were messages more than serious attempts. Rizzo Jr. filed six ethics bills on a single day in 2008, and some of the 27 are a bill paired with its own ballot question. These are 27 bills, not 27 separate campaigns.

Still, bills on the same subjects came back from different members for twenty years and never reached a vote, while every subject on the other list did. Whether these bills died from hostility or neglect, the result is the same. A vote happens when someone with power over the calendar decides it should, and on these subjects, nobody did.

On resign to run, the system worked. Voters said no twice. In February 2026 Council passed a third version 15 to 1, and a month later its sponsor, Isaiah Thomas, moved to repeal it, saying he no longer believed voters would approve. In April Council repealed it and the question came off the ballot. That is a recorded vote to keep a rule on Council in place, and the institution deserves credit for it. But the public got that say only because Council chose to give it. On term limits, public campaign money and a redistricting commission, Council has never asked.

## Can voters go around Council?

Not really. Under the 1949 state law behind the city charter, a 20,000-signature petition for a charter amendment reaches the ballot only if a majority of Council agrees; otherwise "the petition shall be deemed denied." The same number of signatures can force Council to create a commission to write a new charter, but Council's president appoints nine of its fifteen members. That is my reading of the statute's text.

## What I actually want

**A vote on nepotism.** The charter exempts the staff councilmembers appoint from civil service, so those jobs come with no exam and no merit list. State ethics law bars an official from using the office for the financial benefit of a parent, spouse, child, brother or sister. Its definition of family stops there: no cousins, nieces, nephews or in-laws, and no friends or political allies. So picture an office filled with a member's extended family and loyal supporters, qualified or not, every one of them owing a paycheck to one person. That is a power base, and the public pays for it.

A nepotism rule would not stop a member from hiring friends. That is patronage, a bigger fight. But it would draw the first line, and Council has been asked to draw it seven times. One of those bills reached the floor calendar and was never called. Its author, Michael Nutter, imposed the rule on his own branch by executive order after he became mayor, and urged Council "to adopt these policies as legislation." Of the officials outside his branch he said, "they don't work for me." No anti-nepotism bill has been introduced since 2008.

Maybe there is a good case against it. Small offices hire people they trust, and sometimes those people are family. If that is the argument, make it on the floor.

**A rule that forces the question.** Roughly:

- It covers bills on these subjects wherever in the code they are drafted, and the sponsor flags them, so no committee chair decides what counts.
- The committee gets six months after the sponsor asks for a hearing. After that, the bill goes to the full Council anyway.
- Every covered bill gets a recorded vote of the full Council before the term ends.

It does not have to pass. A vote of 0 to 17 tells voters something. Silence tells them nothing.

Two honest problems. Members could vote no and nothing would change, but resign to run shows what a recorded vote makes possible: the public pushed back, and the sponsor withdrew his own bill. And Council writes its own rules, so a rule forcing votes on bills about Council is itself a rule about Council. The sturdier version would go in the charter, which takes 12 of 17 votes to put on the ballot. Late-filed and duplicate bills need handling too, but those are drafting problems, not reasons to keep the silence.

## What to watch

- **Nothing is pending.** I found no bills on these five subjects introduced since January 2024.
- **Resign to run** may come back. Thomas said he might reintroduce it.
- **The 2030 census.** A redistricting commission would need a charter amendment before Council draws the next map.
- **December 2027,** when Jones plans to retire.

The record is public. You do not have to take my reading of it. [Go look](/philadelphia/insights).

**How I counted.** Every bill introduced from 2000 through 2023 that changed a rule for the city's elected officials or the people who deal with them, 123 in all, sorted by subject. "Recorded vote" means a roll call in Legistar at any stage. Committees act without recorded tallies, so a lapsed bill with no roll call never got a final floor vote. The baseline counts bills, not resolutions. Four charter Inspector General proposals also never got a vote; I left them out because it is unclear whether that office would have covered Council. [The full coded list](/data/council-self-rules-2000-2023.csv) has every bill, my call on each, and its official Legistar link.

**Sources.** Jones's DROP plans from the [Inquirer](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/philadelphia/city-councilmember-curtis-jones-representative-jazelle-jones-drop-20260625.html), June 2026. The 2011 DROP override from [CBS Philadelphia](https://www.cbsnews.com/philadelphia/news/philadelphia-city-council-overrides-mayor-nutters-veto-of-drop-pension-program/). Resign to run from the [Inquirer](https://www.inquirer.com/philly/news/politics/20140521_Phila__voters_reject_repealing_resign-to-run_rule.html), [WHYY](https://whyy.org/articles/philly-voters-prefer-city-candidates-to-resign-to-run-for-another-office/), the [Inquirer](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/philadelphia/resign-to-run-repeal-isaiah-thomas-city-council-20260326.html) and [PhillyVoice](https://www.phillyvoice.com/philadelphia-city-council-resign-to-run-law-repeal/). The 2003 pay veto from the [Inquirer](https://www.inquirer.com/philly/news/homepage/20071228_Street_defends_belated_raises.html). Nutter's 2011 orders from [NBC10](https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/politics/mayor-signs-new-ethics-rules/1909406/) and WHYY ([1](https://whyy.org/articles/nutter-signs-ethical-conduct-orders), [2](https://whyy.org/articles/25tmethics/)). Petition routes from sections 2, 3 and 6 of the [First Class City Home Rule Act](https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/LI/US/PDF/1949/0/0155..PDF).
